newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew struggle with yet another breakdown.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew struggle with yet another breakdown.

text.p: The crew of Russia's Mir space station, spinning chaotically in orbit after its computer broke down, is due to try on Tuesday to bring the ship back into line with the sun.
The three man Russian-U.S. crew was forced to shut off all but vital life support systems aboard the 11-year-old station after the computer crashed on Monday during a docking procedure.
The failure meant Mir lost its orientation with the sun, which its solar panels need to face to create energy.

It was the third time the station has spun out of control in less than two months and came as a blow to the new Russian crew, which had had a relatively trouble-free start to their mission after their predecessors suffered a string of disasters.

Despite difficult conditions, Mir's commander Anatoly Solovyov managed to complete the docking of a supply ship manually without incident, but space officials were at a loss to explain the computer breakdown.
Late on Monday the cosmonauts fired booster rockets to push Mir back towards the sun, allowing the station's batteries to charge before they try to reset the orientation.

"It would be better if you did this operation before 11 a.m. tomorrow. If the tests go through, tomorrow we'll set up the orientation," flight director Vladimir Solovyov told Mir during a radio link-up on Monday evening with Mission Control.
An official from NASA, which has an astronaut aboard Mir as part of an international space research programme, said he was confident the crew would be able to fix the problem.

"This is certainly an unfortunate incident," Bob Castle, a NASA space shuttle flight director now in Moscow, told Reuters. "But we know they have recovered from this before, I think they are going to recover from it again."
The previous computer failures took only a day to fix, but space officials said that the latest breakdown meant vital repairs to another part of the station would have to be delayed for a few days.

"With this computer fault today we are bracing ourselves for a tense situation with the battery buffers, our energy reserves," flight director Solovyov told reporters at Mission Control in the town of Korolyov outside Moscow.
"The repairs will be a five-hour-long operation and we cannot begin this operation without coming to terms with what has happened," he said.
Mir has run on partial power since it collided with a previous Progress cargo ship on June 25 in the worst accident in its history.

The computer crashed then and several areas of the station have been out of action since then due to a lack of power. The second computer failure occured on July 17 when an exhausted cosmonaut mistakenly unplugged a vital cable.
Monday's redocking was tense until the last few seconds, and poor visibility added to the woes of commander Anatoly Solovyov, who this month began his fifth flight on Mir.
"I was actually impressed that Solovyov managed to dock the Progress with Mir in free drift; that's not an easy thing to do," said Castle.
